summary: Tobin South, representing WorkOS (an enterprise security vendor) and Stanford's Safe and Useful AI Agents initiative, frames the central question: how do existing enterprise tooling concepts map to AI systems built on MCP? He presents a future architecture where users interact with AI chatbots that call MCP servers, which in turn may invoke cloud-based AI agents, creating multi-layered authentication and authorization challenges. The talk traces a progression from local hacky MCP servers to enterprise-ready deployments. Using a whimsical goat-feeding API turned emotional-support SaaS as a running example, South illustrates each stage's pitfalls: local servers are fun but useless beyond demos; adding authentication and authorization is the first real step; going public introduces payment rails and abuse vectors; and selling into enterprise demands SSO, lifecycle management, provisioning, fine-grained access controls, audit logs, and data loss prevention. South cites Block's Goose as an example of internal MCP provisioning via SSO. Despite progress, significant open questions remain. Remote asynchronous workloads with headless OAuth and dynamic client registration remain super hard. A new MCP elicitation RFC enables models to request human input when stuck. South then addresses a broad unsolved challenge: passing scope and access control between different AI workloads. With A2A protocol, agents mostly communicate in vibes, relying on model alignment rather than robust authorization. Ensuring service accounts have correct access turns out to be a major pain point. Cloud vendors mostly solve hosting, but authorization and access control is the hardest part of putting MCP into external enterprise workloads. WorkOS is actively building this entire stack for AI companies and startups. South closes with a live demo: attendees can buy an MCP-themed shirt only through MCP by adding the server to an AI editor like Cursor, creating an account for authorization, and instructing the agent to purchase. The demo showcases account authorization, bot blocking on signup, address collection, and a successful transaction.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Future Architecture
sections.summary: South introduces the central question of what enterprise-ready MCP means, noting the concept is still nascent. He presents a future architecture where users interact with AI chatbots that call MCP servers, which may in turn invoke cloud-based AI agents, creating multi-layered security and authorization challenges that need to be solved for production use.

sections.title: Speaker Background and WorkOS
sections.summary: South introduces himself as a WorkOS employee, Stanford research fellow on AI agent safety, and recent PhD graduate. WorkOS is an enterprise security vendor that sells to AI labs, providing glue for scaling security and auth operations into the enterprise so agent builders can seamlessly scale.

sections.title: The Goat Example and Why MCP
sections.summary: Using a goat-feeding API turned emotional support SaaS as a running example, South explains why one would move from basic tool calling to MCP: a robust ecosystem of security tooling, standardization for models, stateful connections for better context management, and the fun of building. He notes current tool use is painful and error-prone, motivating MCP's invention.

sections.title: From Local Server to Authentication
sections.summary: South describes the typical MCP building journey: starting with a hacky local server that is only useful to the builder, then adding authentication and authorization as the first essential step. This includes scoping admin privileges, using VPCs for internal deployments, and ensuring no external API is left unauthenticated.

sections.title: Going Public and Scaling Challenges
sections.summary: Making the MCP server public introduces Stripe payment rails, free credits, and cloud hosting. Going viral brings free credit abuse, requiring bot blocking, input validation against prompt injection, and adapted management tooling. MCP's dynamic client registration floods standard OAuth dashboards, meaning every layer of the auth stack needs MCP-specific adaptation.

sections.title: Enterprise Requirements
sections.summary: Selling into enterprise requires SSO, lifecycle management, provisioning, fine-grained access controls, performant audit logs meeting GDPR's AI-specific logging requirements, and data loss prevention. South cites Block's Goose as an example of provisioning MCP access internally via SSO, envisioning enterprises exposing internal resources through MCP for employee workflow automation.

sections.title: Open Questions and Elicitation RFC
sections.summary: South acknowledges that while some parts of the stack are solved, significant open questions remain. Remote asynchronous workloads doing headless OAuth with dynamic client registration are super hard. A new MCP elicitation RFC enables models to request human input when stuck, but the protocol is actively developing and nothing is stable.

sections.title: A2A Scope Passing and Live Shirt Demo
sections.summary: South addresses the broad challenge of passing scope and access control between different AI workloads. With A2A protocol, agents communicate mostly in vibes, relying on model alignment rather than robust authorization, making scope delegation between AI workloads a major pain point. Cloud vendors solve hosting but authorization and access control remain the hardest part of enterprise MCP. WorkOS is actively building this stack for AI companies. South closes with a live demo where attendees buy an MCP-themed shirt only through MCP by adding the server to an AI editor like Cursor, creating an account, and instructing the agent to purchase, showcasing authorization, bot blocking, and successful transaction.
